title: Alto-backed study predicts major economic gains along proposed rail corridor | CBC News
html:
Ottawa

Alto-backed study predicts major economic gains along proposed rail corridor

High-speed rail from Toronto to Quebec City will boost productivity, create jobs, consultant finds

A new study commissioned by the group behind Eastern Canada's proposed high-speed rail line lays out the project's potential to benefit people's lives, their communities and the country's economy if it's done right.

The report argues that Alto will be worth the massive investment because it will boost productivity by better connecting people living and working in the Toronto-Quebec City corridor.

The project was announced late last year with planned stops in Trois-Rivières, Laval, Montreal, Ottawa and Peterborough. Its CEO said this summer that it would likely add a stop in Kingston for some trains.

The government's latest cost estimate is $60 billion to $90 billion, and the federal budget watchdog said recently that could balloon by another $15 billion to $25 billion. Construction would start at the end of this decade or early next decade.

The study by Quebec consultants Aviseo said once fully up and running, Alto would generate about $24.5 billion worth of financial benefits annually by connecting Ontario and Quebec's major population centres.

Workers would have better access to jobs and employers would have a much wider talent pool to draw from if it took an hour or less to commute between Ottawa or Trois-Rivières and Montreal, or Peterborough and Toronto, it said.

Less travel time means more in-person learning, collaboration and networking, plus more leisure time for workers.

Aviseo's 2026 study compares driving times between major population centres along the proposed route, top, with the time it would take aboard an Alto train, bottom. (Aviseo)

That boost to productivity would draw investment and diminish the drag of an aging population on the economy.

"When workers and businesses produce more value per hour worked, wages can rise, prices can fall and governments can collect more revenue without raising tax rates," it said.

'Cost of doing nothing'

According to Aviseo, the growing communities along the proposed route will need to invest something like $50 billion in roads, airports and railways without Alto, and would still not benefit from faster travel between them.

"There's a cost of doing nothing," said Jean-Pierre Lessard, Aviseo's co-founder and partner.

  • Alto high-speed rail project could cost more than originally thought: budget watchdog

  • Montreal-Ottawa high-speed rail line could cross 1,700 properties, Alto predicts

The corridor between Toronto and Quebec City is home to 40 per cent of Canada's population and gross domestic product, but still lacks "a reliable, fast, frequent and affordable way to travel," according to the study.

The anticipated drop in private vehicle traffic that Alto would bring — about 6.8 million fewer trips by 2055, by Aviseo's estimate — would also reduce congestion and collisions.

Alto would also help boost tourism in communities within easy reach of its stations, according to the report.

Loud opposition

There has also been loud opposition to the project, with some warning of serious disruption and the spectre of private land expropriation, with little gain for some regions.

Quebec's premier and the federal Conservatives are against the project, while a source told CBC News in July that the Ontario government is also rethinking its support of Alto.

  • Could Quebec's new government derail plans for Alto's high-speed train project?

  • Quebec farmers challenge costs of Alto high-speed rail, propose new — slower — plan

Aviseo's study, which came the week after a farmer-backed study of a cheaper, slower train line, promises local benefits including a share of the estimated 5,000 jobs related to running and maintaining Alto.

That economic spillover could extend up to 110 kilometres from "station cities," according to the report.

Aviseo said its case studies of other rail projects suggest economic spillover can extend as far as 110 kilometres from a station. This study did not contemplate a stop in Kingston, Ont. (Aviseo)

An Alto spokesperson recently told CBC News that it plans to unveil a narrower proposed corridor between Ottawa and Montreal in the coming weeks.

The Crown corporation also intends to publish a business case early next year.

With files from Dan Taekema and Radio-Canada's Claudine Richard
summary: A new study commissioned by the group behind Eastern Canada's proposed high-speed rail line lays out the project's potential to benefit people's lives, their communities and the region's economy if it's done right.
